Rosai-Dorfman disease has a different histiocytic phenotype and morphology; the CD1a-positive reniform cells support Langerhans cell histiocytosis.
Erdheim-Chester disease is generally CD1a negative and has foamy histiocytes, unlike the reported lesions.
Histiocytosis includes Langerhans cell histiocytosis but omits the required Langerhans-cell subtype.
Sarcoidosis would show noncaseating granulomas rather than a CD1a- and S100-positive reniform-cell infiltrate.
Indeterminate cell histiocytosis is distinct from Langerhans cell histiocytosis and would require subtype-specific evidence such as absent langerin/Birbeck granules.
Purulent discharge and partial antibiotic response may reflect secondary infection, but infection does not explain the diagnostic histology and immunophenotype.

candidate_relations.reason: No evidence supports a myeloproliferative disorder, and this label does not identify the biopsy-proven Langerhans-cell disease.
The biopsy lacks malignant squamous epithelium and instead shows CD1a- and S100-positive mononuclear cells.
Multifocal nail and scalp lesions with reniform mononuclear cells positive for CD1a and S100 are diagnostic of Langerhans cell histiocytosis; BRAF negativity does not exclude it.
Warty dyskeratoma has characteristic epithelial acantholysis and dyskeratosis, not the reported Langerhans-cell infiltrate.
No atypical melanocytic proliferation is described; the immunophenotype and morphology instead support Langerhans cell histiocytosis.
A myxoid cyst cannot account for multifocal nails, scalp papules, or the CD1a- and S100-positive cellular infiltrate.
A myeloproliferative neoplasm is not established by the record and does not match the lesion morphology or immunophenotype.
Juvenile xanthogranuloma is typically CD1a and S100 negative and has xanthomatous or Touton giant-cell morphology.
Histiocytic sarcoma is typically CD68-positive and CD1a-negative, opposite to the reported phenotype, and would show overt cytologic malignancy.
Purulence may indicate superinfection, but infectious nail disease does not explain the multifocal biopsy-proven CD1a- and S100-positive infiltrate.
